segments.title: Opening: The Architecture of Social Triumph

utterances.text: Welcome to Miss Marjoribanks Unpacked — the show that takes one of Victorian fiction's most unjustly overlooked masterpieces and examines it from every angle we can find.
Mrs Oliphant published Miss Marjoribanks in 1866, and it gave the world Lucilla Marjoribanks — a young woman of formidable intelligence, iron will, and absolutely impeccable social manners.

She returns from school to her widowed father's house in the provincial town of Carlingford, announces that she intends to be a comfort to her dear papa, and then proceeds to reorganise everything and everyone in sight.
Today we have three brilliant readers with us to help us understand exactly what Mrs Oliphant was doing with this extraordinary novel.

Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic novels than perhaps any living actor, and he approaches fiction the way a great performer approaches a script — listening for rhythm, timing, the comic machinery hidden in the prose.
There is no one better placed to hear what Oliphant is actually doing sentence by sentence.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don — a literary critic of the old school who reads novels as moral explorations, accounts of character put under pressure.
He brings a rigour, and occasionally a magnificent impatience, that keeps the rest of us honest.
And Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian whose work reads literature as a map of power — who holds the wealth, who holds the social territory, and at whose expense.
In a novel about a woman who sets out to conquer a provincial town, that perspective is going to be indispensable.
Our subject today is the architecture of Lucilla's social triumph — how she builds it, what it costs, and what Oliphant thinks of the whole enterprise.
Oliver — you've spent an enormous amount of time inside this prose.
Where does Lucilla's campaign actually begin — and what does it sound like from the inside?
It begins with a kind of magnificent audacity that I find almost physically pleasurable to read aloud.
Lucilla is barely back in Carlingford before she's deflecting the Rector's attempts to manage her — and she does it with this performance of wide-eyed innocence that is, frankly, hilarious.
The Rector, Mr Bury, has conceived some plan involving a guardian figure for Lucilla — a Mrs Mortimer — and Lucilla completely wrong-foots him.
She fixes him with this earnest gaze and asks:
"Do you mean you have found some one for him to marry?"
She has completely misread the situation — or rather, she has performed a complete misreading, with theatrical precision.
That phrase, "a look of artless surprise" — Oliphant is winking at us the whole time.
Nothing about Lucilla is artless.
What strikes me is that this isn't merely comic strategy — it is a young woman of considerable gifts operating within the only arena available to her.
And Oliphant never lets us forget that tension.
But I want to draw attention to what happens next in that scene — because it shows something more than wit.
Mr Bury is outlining his programme for Lucilla — this poor widow, Mrs Mortimer, as a kind of moral chaperone — and Mrs Mortimer herself begins to look ready to faint.
The Rector cries out in alarm:
"What is the matter?"
And Lucilla simply acts.
She doesn't wring her hands or defer to the Rector — she rings the bell and takes hold of Mrs Mortimer bodily.
This is a portrait of executive competence in a world that has made no provision for it.
And the Rector is simply stranded — Oliphant puts it beautifully.
She writes that Lucilla "took the poor woman by the shoulders and all but lifted her to the sofa" —
"where she was lying down with her bonnet off when the Rector came to his senses."
"To describe the feelings with which Mr Bury contemplated this little entr'acte, which was not in his programme, would be beyond our powers."
Entr'acte — that is a theatrical term, of course, and Oliphant uses it deliberately.
The Rector had a script; Lucilla has just rewritten the second act.
I think we need to be precise about what kind of power Lucilla is wielding and against whom.
The Rector arrives with a plan designed to constrain her — to install a female supervisor over her, a widow whose own precariousness makes her pliable.
This is the institutional church operating as a mechanism of patriarchal control.
And Lucilla defeats it — but she defeats it using the body of another woman.
Mrs Mortimer's fainting fit is the crisis that clears the room, that ends the Rector's address — and Lucilla orchestrates around it with complete efficiency.
What interests me is that Mrs Mortimer is utterly passive throughout — she is both weapon and victim in a game she doesn't understand.
That is rather severe on Lucilla, I think.
She is helping a woman who is about to collapse — that seems to me simply decent.
But I grant you that Lucilla's programme — and that word, programme, recurs throughout the novel — is genuinely ambitious in ways that go far beyond the domestic.
By chapter twenty-three, Oliphant gives us the fullest expression of it — and the passage is almost breathtaking in its scope.
"To vanquish the Archdeacon, to pluck out from the darkness, and rehabilitate and set at his ease the mysterious adventurer" —
"and to finish off by a glorious and triumphant marriage — not her own, it is true, but of her making, which was more to the purpose."
"Not her own, but of her making, which was more to the purpose" — that single clause is Oliphant's whole comedy in miniature.
Lucilla has entirely sublimated personal ambition into social management — and she finds that more satisfying, not less.
The phrase "with the speed of lightning" is doing real work there too.
Lucilla's plans are not deliberated — they are instantaneous, almost involuntary.
Oliphant is suggesting that social calculation, for someone of Lucilla's class and training, is as natural as breathing.
It has been so thoroughly internalised that it no longer feels like strategy — it feels like instinct.
And that is a very precise description of how ideology works.
I'd add one more thing — and it's the moment where the whole machinery clicks most satisfyingly into place.
By chapter twenty-eight, Lucilla has manoeuvred Mr Cavendish back into the social fold — back to Grange Lane — and Oliphant describes the procession with this wonderful mock-heroic grandeur.
Listen to this:
"And it was thus, with Miss Marjoribanks leaning on his arm, and General Travers, in all the warmth of renewed friendship, guarding him on the other side" —
"that Mr Cavendish, whose head was in a whirl of excitement, and who did not know what he was doing, was led back in triumph past Colonel Chiley's very door" —
"where the Archdeacon was lying in wait to crunch his bones, back from all his aberrations into the very heart of Grange Lane."
"Lying in wait to crunch his bones" — that is not the language of a drawing-room comedy.
That's a fairy tale, or a predator's ambush — and Cavendish, poor man, has absolutely no idea it's happening to him.
And that, I think, is the heart of what makes Lucilla so extraordinary and so unsettling — she is always the one who knows what's happening.
Everyone else is in her programme; she alone holds the script.
After the break, we're going to look at exactly how she runs that programme — the day-to-day comedy of what we might call Marjoribanks management, and the people it puts under pressure.

segments.title: Deep Dive: The Comedy of Marjoribanks Management

utterances.text: We've been talking about how Lucilla constructs her social world like an architect — drawing rooms as territory, Thursday evenings as instruments of power.
But architecture requires management — and this is where the comedy lives.
Oliver, you've spent more time than almost anyone alive inside the rhythms of Victorian prose — where does Mrs Oliphant's comic engine really run?
It runs on delay and dread — the two great comic fuels.
Oliphant is essentially a suspense writer in comic clothing.
She builds scenes the way a stage comedian builds a sketch — you know the trap is set, you can see the victim walking towards it, and the pleasure is entirely in the approach.
There's a scene with Mr Cavendish — a man who has, shall we say, a complicated history that Lucilla has quietly uncovered.
She walks him into the darkness — literally, the garden in the dark — and delivers this:
And then — and this is where Oliphant's art is absolutely precise — she gives us his body, not his words.
He turned green in the darkness.
She can't even see his face — and neither can we — but she knows.
What strikes me in that scene is that Lucilla's power over Cavendish isn't malicious — it's almost judicial.
She is, in her way, the moral centre of Carlingford — the person who knows what is owed and to whom.
The comedy is inseparable from her seriousness of purpose.
She sighs — and that sigh finds a terrible echo in his bosom.
The word 'terrible' is carrying enormous weight there.
It is comedy, yes — but it is comedy about guilt and conscience, which is ultimately about character.
I want to hold onto that word 'terrible' as well — but read it differently.
Lucilla's knowledge is power, and in this novel knowledge about people — who they are, where they come from, what they've done — functions as social currency.
She isn't judging Cavendish from some neutral moral position — she's deploying what she knows in order to manage him.
And the comic genius of it — Oliver's absolutely right about the timing — is that she never has to say what she knows.
The threat operates through implication.
That's not just comic craft — that's how social control works in a community without police or courts.
And the management extends to everyone around her — not just those she suspects of secrets.
There's another scene — a beautiful little knife-twist — when Cavendish announces to Barbara Lake that he is going to call on Lucilla.
He says it with a face that extremity has made stolid and impassible — which is about the funniest description of human desperation I have ever read aloud.
And poor Barbara — the colour changed in a moment.
Everything she had counted on collapses in a sentence.
Oliphant is extraordinarily efficient — three characters, one sentence, complete devastation.
The efficiency you're describing is, I think, the mark of a novelist who trusts her readers completely.
She doesn't need to explain Barbara's feelings — the phrase 'her mingled spite and humiliation and mortification' simply lists them and moves on.
There is something almost Augustan in that precision — Johnson would have recognised it as honest writing.
But what I find remarkable is that even here, in what is essentially a comic reversal, Oliphant has sympathy for Barbara.
She calls her 'poor Barbara' — and she means it, even as she's enjoying the scene enormously.
Poor Barbara, yes — but it's worth noting that Barbara's schemes are themselves a form of grasping at resources she has no other way to access.
She doesn't have Lucilla's position, her father's income, her Thursday evenings.
A strategic marriage was one of the very few mechanisms available to women of her standing.
The comedy of Marjoribanks management, as the host put it, often depends on us finding amusing what is actually quite desperate.
And the novel's management of tone is tested most severely when the comedy is interrupted by genuine catastrophe.
Oliver — you've looked at the moment when the Doctor's death reveals something that changes everything about Lucilla's position.
This is where the comedy stops — and where Oliphant shows you she is a much larger writer than a comic novelist.
The Doctor dies — and his will is elaborate, righteous, perfectly just.
And then Oliphant delivers this — and I urge you to listen to every word:
Everything named in it had disappeared like a bubble.
That image — a bubble — is doing the work that another novelist would give an entire chapter.
The richest man — made the poorest — by a single night, a shut door, and silence.
What one feels here is the absolute fragility of the world Lucilla has built.
The Thursday evenings, the carefully managed relationships, the social architecture — all of it rests on a foundation that has simply dissolved.
This is the novel's great moral test — not whom she will marry, but who she is when the resources are gone.
And the phrase 'when he shut his door behind him on that snowy night' — there is such loneliness in it.
The Doctor dying alone, outside, in the snow — and no one knowing until after.
The bubble is the perfect image because it captures how Victorian prosperity actually worked — it looked solid, it felt solid, until the moment it didn't.
The Doctor is not an exception — he is the rule dressed up as an exception.
Wealth in this novel, as in this period, is always partly fiction — and Oliphant knows it.
And then — because Oliphant has an absolute instinct for when the uncanny is needed — there is the bell.
The old disused bell of the Doctor's room — it shouldn't be ringing, it cannot be ringing — and yet it rings.
Rung by a hand too impatient to notice what it was ringing with.
The comedy of management has become something gothic — something that belongs to a different order of feeling entirely.
And yet it is absolutely the same novel — the same voice, the same precision.
The bell is one of those moments in fiction where the metaphorical and the literal are perfectly fused.
It is the Doctor's room, the Doctor's bell, the Doctor's summons — and Lucilla must answer it.
In a sense, the entire latter part of the novel is Lucilla answering that summons — deciding what she owes to his name, his place, his world.
And the summons arrives at precisely the moment when she faces the proposal from Mr Ashburton.
Which is to say — the question of whom she will marry is also a question of what she will become and whether she retains any autonomy at all.
Oliphant gives us that moment of paralysis with extraordinary directness:
For a woman who has known her own mind with extraordinary clarity since the age of seventeen — this is the real catastrophe.
Not the money, not the bell — but not knowing what she wants.
That moment of not-knowing feels like the threshold of something — and it's exactly where we're headed next.
What is Lucilla's inner life, beneath all the management and the mastery — and what does the novel allow her to want?

segments.title: Character and Consequence: The Inner Life of Lucilla

utterances.text: We've been enjoying Lucilla as a comic strategist — the impresario of Thursday evenings, the manager of Carlingford.
But what happens when we look past the performance and into the inner life behind it?
The thing that strikes me every time I return to this novel is how Oliphant refuses to flatten Lucilla.
She is ruthless, yes — but she is also capable of the most disarming tenderness, sometimes within the same paragraph.
There's a passage I keep coming back to — after Lucilla has used poor Mrs Mortimer as what the narrator quite coolly calls a victim.
"though she had not hesitated to sacrifice this poor woman when it was necessary to have a victim, that moment was over, and she had no pleasure in being cruel"
That last clause lands like a moral pardon written in the middle of a crime scene.
Oliphant does not excuse Lucilla. She simply insists we hold both things at once.
Oliver is right, and I think the word the narrator uses — victim — is chosen with full deliberation.
Oliphant is measuring Lucilla against a classical standard of virtue — not condemning her by it, but holding it up beside her.
What we see afterwards is not sentimentality — it is genuine moral recovery.
Lucilla goes and sits with the woman she has just used, and she is — the narrator says — more comforting than the Rector could have been for his life.
That is a precise moral observation. The professional consoler is outperformed by the calculating young woman who still knows how to be kind.
I want to hold onto that word recovery — because I think it does important ideological work in the novel.
Lucilla acts in bad faith toward a woman with no social power whatsoever, and then the narrative rewards her with a scene of warm feeling.
There's something uncomfortable about how efficiently the novel rehabilitates her.
But — and I'll grant this — Oliphant doesn't allow it to become a full absolution. Mrs Mortimer is still displaced. The structural violence is not undone by the kindness.
The tenderness is real and the wound is real. Oliphant is honest enough to leave both standing.
Let me bring in the moment where Lucilla turns the tables on Mr Bury — because this is where you see the sheer reflexive speed of her intelligence.
The narrator says she uttered a scream of genuine alarm and dismay — and then she came to herself, and saw the force of her position.
"She had it in her power to turn the tables on the Rector, and she did not hesitate, as a weaker woman might have done, out of consideration for anybody's feelings."
That phrase — a weaker woman — is doing tremendous work. It is Oliphant's own quiet feminist sting inside the syntax.
The consideration for feelings is what polite society demands of women — and Lucilla simply declines to pay it.
That observation cuts close to the bone, and I think it illuminates why Lucilla is such a difficult figure to place morally.
She is not wicked. She is, in a very precise sense, unwilling to be weak — and Oliphant treats that distinction with great seriousness.
Now — I want to bring in a passage from much later in the novel, where that strength is tested in a quite different register.
Lucilla hears a bell — her father's bell — and the effect on her is devastating.
"Papa's bell! Miss Marjoribanks cried, with a little shriek; and she got up trembling, and then dropped upon her seat again, and in her agitated state burst into tears."
All the controlled management — the strategy, the composure — simply dissolves.
What survives is the daughter. Not the impresario.
That is one of the most striking moments in the novel precisely because it arrives so late — when we've spent hundreds of pages watching Lucilla's will prevail over every obstacle.
And I think the narrator's gloss is quietly devastating — that even so sensible a woman as Lucilla might be justified in fainting.
That word sensible has been used as a kind of armour for Lucilla throughout — and here it becomes almost a term of tenderness.
The grief is unmanaged, unperformed. For once, Lucilla is not staging anything for anyone's benefit.
And then there's poor Tom — who offers perhaps the most painfully authentic emotion in the entire novel.
His proposal — if we can call it that — is a masterpiece of comic suffering.
He manages to stumble through the most important sentence of his life with three successive dashes where the actual word should be.
"I mean I want you to consent to—to—to—marry me, Lucilla. That is what I mean."
That final repetition — That is what I mean — is heartbreaking in its nakedness. He has nothing left to hide behind.
And the dashes are Oliphant's genius — you hear the thing he cannot say, three times, before he finally says it.
Tom is one of those figures novels sometimes produce who are more real than the main action deserves.
And there's something very precise in his lament — I wish to Heaven I was not your cousin.
He identifies the very thing he cannot change as the obstacle — not Lucilla's will, not society's judgment, but the accident of blood.
It is a deeply classical predicament — the man whose fate is written by circumstance, not character.
I'm struck by the Cavendish passage — which shows us quite a different register of Lucilla's inner life.
Because there, the personal and the political are completely entangled in her imagination.
The narrator says she dreamed of Cavendish as member for Carlingford — and then adds, with the addition of other dreams which had not been altogether without their sweetness.

"She would not have been human if she had heard without emotion of the return of the man whom she had once dreamed of as member for Carlingford, with the addition of other dreams which had not been altogether without their sweetness."
That careful phrase — not altogether without their sweetness — is almost a refusal to confess.
Lucilla's ambition and her desire are so intertwined that she herself cannot fully separate them — and neither can the narrator.

What all of these moments share — the snap decision against Mr Bury, the grief at her father's bell, Tom's broken proposal — is that they locate Lucilla's interiority at the exact pressure points where strategy meets feeling.
And that raises a question we haven't yet fully addressed: what does all of this social performance cost — and who pays?
That's the territory we'll move into next — the machinery of class that Lucilla's drawing room both conceals and reveals.

segments.title: The Machinery of Class: Social Critique in Drawing-Room Drama

utterances.text: We've been exploring Lucilla's inner life — her ambitions, her contradictions, the surprising depth beneath her social performance.
But that performance doesn't happen in a vacuum — it operates within, and upon, a very specific social machinery.
Daniel, you've been champing at the bit, I suspect — let's talk about what Oliphant is actually doing with class in this novel.
What strikes me most is how Oliphant makes the management of social space inseparable from the management of people — and people sorted very precisely by rank.
Lucilla's Thursday evenings aren't entertainment — they're a system of controlled circulation, where every movement has a consequence.
Take this moment in Chapter Twenty-Eight, where Lucilla extracts Mr Cavendish from Barbara Lake's company.
Every word is a calculated instrument — the apology, the dismissal, the kiss on the unwilling cheek.
Rose Lake is beneath Lucilla's social station, and Lucilla knows it — but she requires Rose's musical talent to run her evenings.
That kiss is not affection — it is compensation, rendered in the currency of condescension.
I take the point — but I confess, when I read that passage aloud, what I feel first is the sheer comic nerve of it.
Lucilla says she is very sorry, and you know perfectly well she is not in the least sorry.
The gap between the stated sentiment and the ruthless action — that's where Oliphant lives as a writer.
And then — the unwilling cheek.
Poor Rose can't even object — she has to stand there and receive Lucilla's affection like a package being delivered.
There's cruelty in it, yes — but Oliphant is laughing, and so are we, and I think that's rather the point.
I would resist the temptation to flatten this into a diagram of class mechanics, if I may.
Lucilla is a woman of exceptional practical intelligence operating in a world where women have almost no formal power.
What looks like condescension is, in another light, the only currency available to her.
Oliphant is not endorsing the system — she is showing us, with considerable irony, the woman who has mastered it precisely because she had no alternative.
Edmund, I don't disagree — but I'd push further.
Because there's a moment in Chapter Thirty-Two that reveals exactly how precarious the whole edifice is — and who gets crushed when it wobbles.
The Archdeacon arrives at one of Lucilla's dinners and sees, across the room, a man he knows to be an impostor.
Full in the light of the lamp — Oliphant stages this like a theatrical exposure.
Cavendish has been laundered by Lucilla's social approval — her drawing-room is, quite literally, the mechanism that has made him respectable.
And when that approval fails, the crash is instantaneous.
That phrase — 'his favourite adventurer' — is extraordinary, isn't it.
There's something almost fond in it — the Archdeacon has been waiting for this moment, relishing it in advance.
Oliphant gives the Archdeacon a kind of grim satisfaction that is wonderfully human and just slightly disreputable.
But what I find most interesting is Lucilla's response — not Cavendish's, not the Archdeacon's.
She retreats to the drawing-room with the women and stands by the door, watching the staircase.
'A set of men left to themselves' — she doesn't trust men to manage anything without her supervision.
It's terrifying and hilarious in equal measure.
That passage is one of the finest comic observations in the novel, I think — and one should not be too quick to leave the comedy behind.
Lucilla's anxiety is entirely genuine — but what she fears is disorder, not injustice.
She is, in the deepest sense, a conservative — a preserver of forms.
And that conservatism is precisely what gives her power — and precisely what limits it.
Which brings me to the election chapters — and Mr Ashburton's address to the enlightened electors of Carlingford.
This is where the novel's social critique becomes, I would argue, almost savage.
Ashburton speaks to the voters, and here is what he says:
And Oliphant adds — with perfect deadpan — that at this very moment he had in his pocket another address, in which he had entered at some length into his distinctive personal views.
The gap between the public speech and the private document — that is, between performance and reality — is the novel's political argument in miniature.
Carlingford's 'enlightened' electorate is flattered precisely so that it will ask no questions.
The 'daring candidate' — Oliphant calls him 'the daring candidate' immediately after that speech.
The irony is just dripping off the page.
The daring consists entirely in saying nothing while appearing to say something rather brave.
I think Oliphant is being rather harder on the voters than on the candidate, if we're honest.
Ashburton simply offers what is being asked for — the comfortable illusion of the independent, incorruptible gentleman.
And Lucilla — who has managed the whole campaign — is the one who understands most clearly what the voters actually want.
And then — at the very height of her power, when Lucilla has apparently won — everything is annihilated.
Her father dies and the money is gone — and what Oliphant shows us is not grief, exactly, but a kind of total erasure of possibility.
Here is the sentence Oliphant writes — and it is, I think, one of the most devastating in the novel:
The plans she 'thought so wicked' — her half-formed hopes for her own future — extinguished not by grief but by sheer incomprehension.
And the word 'amaze' — that dull amaze — tells us everything about a system that has left this brilliant woman with no resource of her own.
The social machinery that she ran so expertly turns out to have been running her all along.
'To which no words could give any expression' — that silence at the heart of the sentence is something a novelist earns over four hundred pages.
Oliphant has talked about Lucilla at such length, with such precision, that when the words give out, you feel it physically.
That is not something you do with craft — that is something you do with genius.
I find myself, on this point, in complete agreement with Daniel — which is an unusual position for me.
The novel has been, throughout, a comedy of manners — and Oliphant earns that crash into the tragic register precisely because she has never cheated.
Lucilla's vulnerability was always there, underneath the management — we simply weren't allowed to look directly at it.
All of which raises a question about the narrator who has been orchestrating our view of all this — allowing us to see certain things clearly, and obscuring others.
After the break, we'll turn to Oliphant's narrative technique — the invisible hand that has been guiding us through Carlingford all along.

segments.title: Narrative Technique and the Omniscient Eye

utterances.text: We've been tracking how Oliphant uses social machinery to reveal and conceal power — now I want to turn to the instrument doing all that revealing and concealing: the narrator herself.
Because the narrative voice in Miss Marjoribanks is one of the most unusual things about this novel — omniscient, yes, but with an irony so finely calibrated it's almost impossible to pin down.
Edmund, you've been sitting with several of the passages that put that narrative voice most on display — where would you like to begin?
I'd like to begin with what I think is the most deceptively simple sentence in the passages I've been given.
It comes after Lucilla's second Thursday evening — the occasion on which Barbara Lake has behaved in a way that unsettles Carlingford's social order.
The narrator says — and I want to read this quite carefully —

"Perhaps it would be false to say that she had suffered in the course of this second Thursday, or that a superior intelligence like Lucilla's could permit itself to feel any jealousy of Barbara Lake; but it would be vain to deny that she had been surprised."
That word — surprised — is doing extraordinary work.
The narrator refuses to allow Lucilla suffering, refuses to allow her jealousy — both would diminish the character she has constructed — and yet cannot quite suppress the evidence.
And then comes that magnificent follow-on: "any one who knows Miss Marjoribanks will acknowledge that a great deal was implied in that confession."
The narrator is simultaneously Lucilla's advocate, Lucilla's biographer, and — with perfect courtesy — Lucilla's most penetrating critic.
That triple role is exactly right, and from a performance standpoint it creates an almost impossible challenge — because the voice has to hold all three at once.
When I encounter a narrator like this one, I think of her as a character in her own right — one with a very definite personality and a very particular relationship to her subject.

And what strikes me about the passage Edmund read is the rhythm of the denial — "perhaps it would be false... it would be vain to deny" — those elegant hedges that somehow confirm everything they appear to dismiss.
Oliphant has constructed a narrator who protests too much, and knows she protests too much, and wants us to know that she knows.
It's triple irony — which is very difficult to read aloud without collapsing into a smirk.
I want to add a dimension to this, because I think the narrative voice is also — and not incidentally — a voice that manages information the way Lucilla manages her drawing room.
Consider what happens at the dinner table in chapter thirty-two, when Lucilla has to physically redirect the Archdeacon.
The narrator gives us the action — "she put her hand upon his arm sharply, and with a certain energy" — and then the speech itself:
"Mr Beverley, Thomas is behind you with the soup."
Five words of social control delivered as domestic instruction.
And the narrator's description of what follows — "when he had met Miss Marjoribanks's eye the Archdeacon sat down" — that is the real payload.
No explanation of how she does it, no analysis of the power — just the fact of it, dropped into the sentence as though it were the most natural thing in the world.
The narrator normalises Lucilla's authority precisely by refusing to question it.
Daniel's point about normalisation is sharp, but I'd frame it differently.
The narrator doesn't question Lucilla's authority because she — like us — has come to regard Lucilla as a force of nature rather than a social actor.
And that, I think, is the great comic achievement of the narrative technique: we are made complicit in admiring someone we are simultaneously gently mocking.
The passage about the election colours is where the comedy becomes almost philosophical.
Lucilla tells Mr Ashburton — and the narrator records this with perfect deadpan —
"I was not thinking of Reform. I was thinking what your colours were to be. I would not have anything to do with the old colours, for my part — they would be as bad as opinions, you know."
"They would be as bad as opinions" — there is a whole theory of Carlingford politics in that clause.
And the narrator gives it to us without so much as raising an eyebrow — which is, of course, the most devastating possible response.
"As bad as opinions" — I've read that line perhaps a dozen times and it still lands differently every time.
The genius of it is that Lucilla means it sincerely, and the narrator knows she means it sincerely, and the narrator also knows that we know it's absurd.
That triangulation between character, narrator, and reader — it's what makes the comic timing work on the page the way it would work on stage.
Now, where the narrator's voice shifts — genuinely shifts into something warmer — is the passage about forbearance in chapter forty-seven.
The narrator tells us, and here I want to be careful with the phrasing:

"She had been making an effort over herself, and she had come out of it triumphant; after reading so many good books, it is not to be wondered at if she felt herself a changed and softened and elevated character."
"After reading so many good books" — the irony is still there, still entirely present, and yet something else has crept in.
There is a real tenderness toward Lucilla in that sentence — a narrator who has watched this woman manoeuvre for years and finds herself moved by the moment of genuine moral choice.
I think Oliver is right that the narrator's temperature changes there, and I'd locate the reason in the political situation of that chapter.
Lucilla has power — real, consequential power — over a man's political prospects, and she chooses not to use it.
The narrator says plainly: "She had the means in her hands of doing her candidate's rival a deadly mischief, and yet, for old friendship's sake, Lucilla made up her mind to forbear."
Now, from my angle, what is interesting here is that this is one of the few moments where Lucilla's power is entirely hers — not mediated through a dinner table, not licensed by her father.
And what does she do with it?
She renounces it — for friendship, for old loyalty, for something the novel treats as genuinely virtuous.
The narrator's warmth here isn't sentimental — it's the recognition that Lucilla has, for once, stepped outside the transactional logic that governs Carlingford.
And then the novel saves its most extraordinary narrative move for the very end — or near the end — when the voice cracks.
The passage in chapter fifty, when Lucilla's composure finally fails her — not before a great drama, not before a crisis of society — but before Tom.
And the narrator steps forward, drops the ironic mask, and simply says:
"It is hard to have to wind up with such a confession after having so long entertained a confidence in Lucilla which nothing seemed likely to impair."
"It is hard" — the narrator speaks of her own difficulty.
Not Lucilla's difficulty — the narrator's.
That is a startling admission — the voice has been so thoroughly invested in Lucilla that her failure is felt as the narrator's own.
It is, I think, as moving a moment of narrative honesty as anything in Victorian fiction.
When I read that passage aloud — and I have — I always pause after "it is hard."
Because the sentence has weight that the irony has been suppressing for four hundred pages, and when it comes out, you need a moment to let it settle.
What Oliphant has done across this novel is use the narrator as a kind of pressure valve — releasing just enough warmth at just the right moment to stop the whole thing becoming cold.
And then that warmth catches you completely off guard — which is of course when it works best.
The narrator confiding her own difficulty — her own investment in a character she's spent the novel both championing and quietly dismantling.
That's a very particular kind of literary intimacy — and it sets up beautifully what we turn to next.

Because that confidence Lucilla entertains — and that the narrator has been protecting — is about to be tested by the entanglements of the Cavendish affair, with its secrets, its scandal, and its very sharp consequences for the people Lucilla thought she understood best.

segments.title: Scandal and Consequence: The Cavendish and Marjoribanks Entanglements

utterances.text: We've been tracing how Oliphant's narrator holds Lucilla at arm's length — watching her with an almost surgical detachment.
Now we see what happens when that composure is actually tested — when the social machinery Lucilla has built threatens to fly apart.
The scene with Miss Bury is one of the great comic set-pieces in the novel — and it turns on a single, perfectly terrible question.
Miss Bury asks poor Tom whether he believes in Jove — and the narrator gives us this, verbatim:
"The unfortunate Tom grew red and then he grew green under this question and that awful look."
Red and then green — that is the complete spectrum of social mortification, rendered in two colours.
And then the barrister — the 'amusing man' — laughs.
Not supportively — the narrator is very precise — it is unsympathetic laughter.
Oliphant knows exactly how unkind laughter sounds, and how it lands in a room.
What strikes me is how the narrator characterises this as a test of character — not merely a social inconvenience.
The passage tells us, with that slightly wry formality Oliphant does so well:

"There could not have been a more unfortunate contretemps, and there is no telling how disastrous the effect might have been, had not her courage and coolness, not to say her orthodoxy, been equal to the occasion."
Note that word — orthodoxy.
Oliphant places it alongside courage and coolness as a civic virtue — not a theological one.
Lucilla's social genius is inseparable from her conformity to established forms — she would not function without them.
That is not satirised here — it is presented as genuinely admirable, a strength of will.
I'd push back on that slightly.
The narrator is admiring Lucilla, yes — but the comedy is not entirely warm.
The 'orthodoxy' that saves her is the orthodoxy of a deeply exclusionary social order.
Tom's humiliation comes precisely from stepping outside the ritual — from failing the performance.
And what restores order is not kindness — it is Lucilla 'taking affairs into her own hands,' reasserting the rules that protect her position.
The anxiety doesn't vanish with the recovery, though — it haunts Lucilla's sleep.

There's a genuinely strange dream sequence where Lucilla stands at the altar, and Mr Bury — with inflexible cruelty, as the narrator puts it — insists on marrying her to Tom Marjoribanks instead of Mr Cavendish.
And then the dream shifts — Cavendish does not win the parliamentary seat.
Instead it is the amusing man, as the defeated candidate, who grins at her from the hustings and — here the narrator is wickedly specific —
"said from the hustings that he would never forget the luncheon that had been his first introduction to Carlingford."
The luncheon follows her even into sleep — it is Lucilla's version of the Scottish play.
That dream is psychologically acute in a way the novel doesn't always announce.
The two anxieties collapse into one — the wrong marriage and the public humiliation — which tells us something about what Lucilla actually fears.
She does not fear poverty, or isolation, or unhappiness in any private sense.
She fears being the figure that a man mocks publicly — the failure of her design.
Which brings us to Cavendish himself — who is not exactly an innocent party in all this.
Look at what the duet does to him in the drawing room.
The narrator describes the moment with an almost military precision:

"The words were arrested on the very lips of the talkers; Mrs Woodburn paused in the midst of doing Lucilla, and, as we have before said, Mr Cavendish broke a flirtation clean off at its most interesting moment."
Clean off — that phrase is doing serious work.
The flirtation is a transaction — and Lucilla's music simply outbids it.
Culture here is not pleasure — it is power, wielded with complete deliberation.
And Mrs Woodburn pausing in the midst of doing Lucilla — that's exquisite.
The mimic is silenced by the original — it is the best possible revenge, and Lucilla hasn't even aimed it deliberately.
Or perhaps she has — with Lucilla one is never entirely sure.
The Cavendish entanglement reaches its most interesting point when the political and matrimonial ambitions become genuinely indistinguishable.
He congratulates Lucilla on her social politics — and the narrator frames it with that comic understatement Oliphant relishes.
Cavendish says to her:
"your conception of social politics, it is masterly"
Masterly — not charming, not clever.
He is acknowledging a rival intelligence, which means — whether he knows it or not — he is already half-defeated.
And yet the narrator is precise about what Lucilla actually feels — which is not triumph, but obligation.
The passage tells us that when a young man who intends to go into Parliament compliments a young lady on her statesmanlike views —
"it must be confessed that it looks a little particular; and then, if that was what he meant, it was no doubt Lucilla's duty to make up her mind."
Her duty — not her desire.
That is the iron cage the novel keeps rattling — Lucilla's ambitions are enormous, but the only socially available form for them is marriage.
She approaches even that as a strategic problem — and the narrator, to her credit, refuses to sentimentalise it.
Duty, strategy, and a triumph that may cost more than it yields — that question of what Lucilla's success actually amounts to is exactly where we're headed next.
The final segment asks: when Lucilla gets what she's worked for, is it enough — and what has she given up to get it?

segments.title: Closing: The Triumph and Its Costs

utterances.text: What we've been tracing, really, is a long game — Lucilla's strategic patience across a decade of Carlingford's social life.
So let's ask the question this final chapter forces on us: what does the triumph actually cost her, and what does it mean?
I think we have to begin at the beginning — at the breakfast table, very early in the novel, where everything Lucilla is going to do is already in motion.
She has taken the Doctor's seat — quite literally displaced the man of the house — and she does it so smoothly that he barely registers what has happened.
The narrator's description of that moment is, I think, one of the finest sentences in the novel.
"he became aware all the same that he had abdicated, without knowing it, and that the reins of state had been smilingly withdrawn from his unconscious hands."
The word "abdicated" is doing enormous work there — it is the language of monarchs, of constitutional crisis.
And yet it happens over a tea urn, managed with a smile.
Oliphant is telling us that this is how power actually changes hands — not in grand scenes of confrontation, but invisibly, domestically, smilingly.
And the Doctor just says "Humph!" — which is, honestly, one of the great single-word lines in Victorian fiction.
He knows something has happened. He can't quite name it. And Oliphant doesn't let him.
That disproportion — the weightiest of political language applied to the most domestic of acts — is where the comedy and the critique are completely inseparable.
And it sets up everything that follows for the next forty-odd chapters.
What strikes me is that Lucilla's victories throughout the novel are always victories over constraint, not over rivals.
And the narrator is quite clear-eyed about what those constraints look like on the inside — particularly when it comes to the question of love and ambition.
There's a passage after the Archdeacon episode that I keep returning to — the narrator's gloss on what Lucilla has actually lost.
"She was not in love with the Archdeacon, any more than she had been in love with Mr Cavendish;—though it is true, love is not everything."
That final clause — "love is not everything" — is the most loaded parenthesis in the book.
It is simultaneously Lucilla's defence, Oliphant's sympathy, and a quiet indictment of a world that has made love into the only currency a woman is supposed to trade in.
Lucilla's genius has nowhere to go except inward — into management, into social arrangement, into the urn and the Thursday evenings.
I would gently resist the word indictment — though I take Daniel's point about the constraint.
What I find more interesting is the tenderness Oliphant allows Lucilla in those unguarded moments — particularly around Tom.
There is a passage where the narrator observes something almost paradoxical — that this woman of extraordinary intelligence finds genuine comfort in pitying a far simpler man.
"She was a woman of genius, and he only a very simple, unlucky fellow; and yet a sensation of comfort came to Lucilla's heart when she said 'Poor Tom!'"
That is not satire — or not only satire.
That is genuine psychological insight into how a great nature can find rest in something smaller than itself.
Oliphant earns that tenderness — she does not simply bestow it.
"Poor Tom" — three syllables that do extraordinary things.
There's condescension in it, certainly — but also real affection, and something close to relief.
Lucilla has spent a decade being cleverer than every room she walks into — and Tom doesn't ask her to be anything but herself.
That's the secret of the ending, I think — and it is an ending that the novel earns, which not all comic novels do.
I want to sit with the final chapter for a moment — because the closing image of Lucilla and Tom is both triumphant and, I think, quietly elegiac.
Look at what the narrator is actually cataloguing when she summons up all the obstacles — the archdeacons, the doctors, the generals, the members of Parliament.
"after all the archdeacons, doctors, generals, members of Parliament—after the ten years and more in which she had not gone off"
"Not gone off" — that phrase carries the whole social structure on its back.
A woman of obvious genius, described in market terms — as though she were a commodity with a limited shelf life.
The fact that Oliphant uses the phrase with such cheerful irony doesn't neutralise it — it makes it more devastating.
And yet "It was to be Tom after all" — that sentence lands, doesn't it?
"Fate and honest love had been waiting all the time till their moment came; and now it was not even necessary to say anything about it."
"Honest love" — not brilliant love, not passionate love.
Oliphant is not settling for a conventional happy ending — she is saying something quite specific about what sustains a life.
Lucilla, who has managed everything and everyone for a decade, finally submits — if that is even the right word — to something that has simply waited for her.
There is wisdom in that, I think — and Oliphant is wise enough not to over-explain it.
"It was to be Tom after all." Five words.
The whole novel — ten years, dozens of schemes, a drawing room run like a state — and it ends on five words.
That is a writer who knows exactly when to stop performing and let the story breathe.
Oliphant earns every syllable of that quiet.
I think that's the perfect place to pause — on that quiet, and on what it contains.
What this conversation has shown, I think, is just how much is packed into Miss Marjoribanks — the comedy, the ambition, the social architecture, the tenderness tucked beneath the satire.
Oliver, Edmund, Daniel — thank you.
You've brought this novel to life in ways that I think would have delighted Mrs Oliphant — who knew better than most that being underestimated is its own kind of power.
And to our listeners — thank you for spending time in Carlingford.
It is a small town with very large inhabitants — and Lucilla Marjoribanks is the largest of them all.

c8:p45.text:
"Do
you mean you have found some one for him to marry?" she asked, with a
look of artless surprise, bending her earnest gaze on Mr Bury's face.
c8:p45.summary: Lucilla feigns artless misunderstanding, asking if Mr Bury has found a remarriage prospect for her father.
c8:p45.best_quote: Do you mean you have found some one for him to marry?

c8:p56.text:
You may think the liberty is pleasant at first, but if you
had a Christian friend to watch over and take care of you——What is the
matter?" said the Rector, in great alarm. It was only that the poor
widow who was to have charge of Lucilla, according to his benevolent
intention, looked so like fainting, that Miss Marjoribanks jumped up
from her chair and rang the bell hastily.
c8:p56.summary: As Mr Bury outlines his plan, Mrs Mortimer looks ready to faint, forcing Lucilla to ring the bell and intervene with practical concern.

c8:p57.text:
It was not Lucilla's way to
lose time about anything; she took the poor woman by the shoulders and
all but lifted her to the sofa, where she was lying down with her bonnet
off when the Rector came to his senses. To describe the feelings with
which Mr Bury contemplated this little  entr'acte , which was not in his
programme, would be beyond our powers.
c8:p57.summary: Lucilla efficiently takes charge, helping the fainting Mrs Mortimer to the sofa while the Rector watches helplessly, unable to proceed with his address.

c23:p118.text:
To vanquish the Archdeacon, to pluck out from the darkness,
and rehabilitate and set at his ease the mysterious adventurer, whom, to
be sure,  she could not say she knew —for Lucilla was very careful,
even in her own thoughts, not to commit herself on this subject—and to
finish off by a glorious and triumphant marriage—not her own, it is
true, but of her making, which was more to the purpose—such was the
programme she made out for herself with the speed of lightning, the
moment she had laid hold of the clue which guided or seemed to guide her
through the labyrinth.

c28:p89.text:
And
it was thus, with Miss Marjoribanks leaning on his arm, and General
Travers, in all the warmth of renewed friendship, guarding him on the
other side, that Mr Cavendish, whose head was in a whirl of excitement,
and who did not know what he was doing, was led back in triumph past
Colonel Chiley's very door, where the Archdeacon was lying in wait to
crunch his bones, back from all his aberrations into the very heart of
Grange Lane.

c28:p68.text:
"Yes," said Miss Marjoribanks, with a certain solemnity, interrupting
him; "I have been thinking a great deal—and  hearing  a great deal
about you, Mr Cavendish." When she had said this Lucilla sighed, and her
sigh found a terrible echo in her hearer's bosom. She knew that he
turned green in the darkness as he gave an anxious look at her. But he
was too much alarmed to give her an opportunity of studying his face.

c30:p15.text:
"Yes, I am going to see Miss Marjoribanks," he said, with a face
which extremity rendered stolid and impassible. As for poor Barbara, her
colour changed in a moment. The very least that she had a right to
expect was that he should have asked her pardon, put himself at her
feet; and her mingled spite and humiliation and mortification at this
response were beyond telling.
c30:p15.summary: Mr Cavendish admits his intention to visit Lucilla, shocking Barbara into an emotional transformation from manipulative to devastated.
c30:p15.best_quote: Yes, I am going to see Miss Marjoribanks

c43:p53.text:
He was dead, and he had made an elaborate will, which was all as just
and righteous as a will could be; but after the will was read, it was
found out that everything named in it had disappeared like a bubble. Instead of being the richest, Dr Marjoribanks was one of the poorest
men in Carlingford when he shut his door behind him on that snowy night.

c49:p71.text:
The old disused bell that had so often called Dr
Marjoribanks up at night, and which hung near the door of the old
Doctor's room, just over the drawing-room, began to peal through the
silence, as if rung by a hand too impatient to notice what it was with
which it made its summons.
c49:p71.summary: The long-disused bell of Lucilla's late father summons from above, pealing urgently as if rung by an impatient hand.

c49:p26.text:
For the first time in her life she not
only did not know what she would do, but she did not know what she
wanted to do. There could now be no mistaking what Mr Ashburton's
intentions were. Up to a very recent time Lucilla had been able to take
refuge in her mourning, and conclude that she had no present occasion to
disturb herself. But now that calm was over.
c49:p26.summary: Lucilla recognises that Mr Ashburton intends a proposal and faces an unprecedented crisis of indecision about her true desires.
c49:p26.best_quote: For the first time in her life she not only did not know what she would do, but she did not know what she wanted to do

c8:p69.text:
When he was gone Miss Marjoribanks felt the full importance of
her victory; and then, though she had not hesitated to sacrifice this
poor woman when it was necessary to have a victim, that moment was over,
and she had no pleasure in being cruel; on the contrary, she went and
sat by her patient, and talked, and was very kind to her; and after a
while heard all her story, and was more comforting than the Rector could
have been for his life.
c8:p69.summary: Once her victory is assured, Lucilla abandons her calculated coldness and becomes genuinely kind to the suffering Mrs Mortimer, sitting with her and offering comfort.

c8:p44.text:
Lucilla uttered a scream of genuine alarm and dismay; and then she came
to herself, and saw the force of her position. She had it in her power
to turn the tables on the Rector, and she did not hesitate, as a weaker
woman might have done, out of consideration for anybody's feelings.
c8:p44.summary: Lucilla gasps in alarm at Mr Bury's suggestion, then quickly recognizes the opportunity to turn the tables on him.

c49:p72.text:
"Papa's bell!" Miss Marjoribanks cried, with a little shriek; and she
got up trembling, and then dropped upon her seat again, and in her
agitated state burst into tears. And Mr Ashburton felt that, under these
most extraordinary circumstances, even so sensible a woman as Lucilla
might be justified in fainting, embarrassing and uncomfortable as that
would be.
c49:p72.summary: Lucilla recognises the bell as her late father's summons and bursts into tears at the revelation.
c49:p72.best_quote: "Papa's bell!" Miss Marjoribanks cried, with a little shriek; and she got up trembling, and then dropped upon her seat again, and in her agitated state burst into tears

c9:p41.text:
"Lucilla," cried the unlucky fellow, "is it possible that you really
have misunderstood me all this time? Do you mean to say that you don't
know? Oh, Lucilla, listen just five minutes. It isn't because I am your
cousin. I wish to Heaven I was not your cousin, but some one you had
never seen before. I mean I want you to consent to—to—to—marry me,
Lucilla. That is what I mean.
c9:p41.summary: Tom finally explicitly proposes marriage, admitting his long-held love and his wish that he were not her cousin, begging Lucilla to listen to him.
c9:p41.best_quote: I mean I want you to consent to—to—to—marry me, Lucilla.

c38:p62.text:
But this news was naturally much more serious to Miss Marjoribanks when
she got upstairs, and had time to think of it. She would not have been
human if she had heard without emotion of the return of the man whom she
had once dreamed of as member for Carlingford, with the addition of
other dreams which had not been altogether without their sweetness.
c38:p62.summary: Lucilla recognizes that Mr Cavendish's return stirs emotions she thought past—he had been her dream candidate and romantic interest.
c38:p62.best_quote: She would not have been human if she had heard without emotion of the return of the man whom she had once dreamed of as member for Carlingford, with the addition of other dreams which had not been altogether without their sweetness.

c28:p50.text:
"I am very sorry to separate you from Barbara," said Miss Marjoribanks;
"but she is at home, you know, and I want so much to talk to you. Barbara, good-night; I want Mr Cavendish to walk home with me. Rose,
don't stand in the garden and catch cold; thank you, dear, for such a
pleasant evening," said Lucilla, pressing another kiss upon her little
friend's unwilling cheek.

c32:p22.text:
When he raised his
head and looked round him, naturally Mr Beverley's eyes went direct to
the mark like an arrow; he looked, and he saw at the centre of the
table, surrounded by every kind of regard and consideration, full in the
light of the lamp, his favourite adventurer, the impostor whom he had
denounced the first time he took his place by Miss Marjoribanks's side.

c32:p48.text:
And Lucilla certainly was not herself for
the first half-hour. She kept close to the door, and regarded the
staircase with an anxious countenance. When she was herself at the helm
of affairs, there was a certain security that everything would go on
tolerably—but nobody could tell what a set of men left to themselves
might or might not do. This was the most dreadful moment of the evening.
c32:p48.summary: Lucilla's composure cracks in the drawing-room; she anxiously awaits the men, fearing uncontrolled conversation.
c32:p48.best_quote: When she was herself at the helm of affairs, there was a certain security that everything would go on tolerably—but nobody could tell what a set of men left to themselves might or might not do

c37:p77.text:
"The enlightened electors of Carlingford do not demand,
like other less educated constituencies, a system of political doctrines
cut and dry, or a representative bound to give up his own judgment, and
act according to arbitrary promises," said the daring candidate: "what
they want is an honest man, resolved to do his duty by his country, his
borough, and his constituency; and it is this idea alone which has
induced me to solicit your suffrages." This was what Mr Ashburton said
in his address, though at that moment he had still his other address in
his pocket, in which he had entered at some length into his distinctive
personal views.

c43:p54.text:
It was a revelation which took the town perfectly by storm, and startled
everybody out of their senses. Lucilla's plans, which she thought so
wicked, went out all of a sudden, in a certain dull amaze and dismay, to
which no words could give any expression. Such was the second
inconceivable reverse of fortune which happened to Miss Marjoribanks,
more unexpected, more incomprehensible still than the other, in the very
midst of her most important activities and hopes.
c43:p54.summary: Lucilla's carefully suppressed hopes for her future are instantly extinguished by the revelation of her father's financial ruin, which is even more incomprehensible than his death.
c43:p54.best_quote: Lucilla's plans, which she thought so wicked, went out all of a sudden, in a certain dull amaze and dismay, to which no words could give any expression

c12:p43.text:
Perhaps it
would be false to say that she had suffered in the course of this second
Thursday, or that a superior intelligence like Lucilla's could permit
itself to feel any jealousy of Barbara Lake; but it would be vain to
deny that she had been  surprised . And any one who knows Miss
Marjoribanks will acknowledge that a great deal was implied in that
confession.

c12:p43.best_quote: "Perhaps it would be false to say that she had suffered in the course of this second Thursday, or that a superior intelligence like Lucilla's could permit itself to feel any jealousy of Barbara Lake; but it would be vain to deny that she had been surprised."

c32:p24.text:
She put her hand
upon his arm sharply, and with a certain energy. "Mr Beverley, Thomas is
behind you with the soup," said Miss Marjoribanks. The Archdeacon turned
round to see what it was, conscious that somebody had spoken to him, but
as indifferent to his companion and to civility as he was to Thomas and
the soup. "What?" he said hoarsely, interrupting his scrutiny for the
moment. But when he had met Miss Marjoribanks's eye the Archdeacon sat

Lucilla smiled compassionately, and with the gentlest tolerance, at this
wild suggestion. "I was not thinking of Reform," she said, with that
meekness which people assume when it is of no use being impatient. "I
was thinking what your colours were to be. I would not have anything to
do with the old colours, for my part—they would be as bad as opinions,
you know. You may laugh, but I am quite in earnest," said Miss
Marjoribanks.

I would not have anything to do with the old colours, for my part—they would be as bad as opinions, you know. You may laugh, but I am quite in earnest, said Miss Marjoribanks.

c47:p67.text:
She had been making an effort over herself, and she had
come out of it triumphant; after reading so many good books, it is not
to be wondered at if she felt herself a changed and softened and
elevated character. She had the means in her hands of doing her
candidate's rival a deadly mischief, and yet, for old friendship's sake,
Lucilla made up her mind to forbear.

She had the means in her hands of doing her candidate's rival a deadly mischief, and yet, for old friendship's sake, Lucilla made up her mind to forbear.

c50:p44.text:
But now, when it was only
Tom—he whom, once upon a time, she had dismissed with affectionate
composure, and given such excellent advice to, and regarded in so
motherly a way—all Lucilla's powers seemed to fail her. It is hard to
have to wind up with such a confession after having so long entertained
a confidence in Lucilla which nothing seemed likely to impair.
c50:p44.summary: The narrator laments having to confess that Lucilla's emotions have finally been engaged, breaking her previous pattern.
c50:p44.best_quote: It is hard to have to wind up with such a confession after having so long entertained a confidence in Lucilla which nothing seemed likely to impair.

c7:p48.text:
The unfortunate Tom grew red and then he grew green under this question
and that awful look. "No, Miss Bury, I can't say I do," he answered
humbly; and the amusing man was so much less brotherly than Tom that he
burst into unsympathetic laughter. As for Lucilla, it was the first real
check she had sustained in the beginning of her career.
c7:p48.summary: Tom is mortified by Miss Bury's question and admits he does not believe in Jove; the barrister laughs unkindly, and Lucilla faces her first real check.
c7:p48.best_quote: The unfortunate Tom grew red and then he grew green under this question and that awful look.

c7:p49.text:
There could not
have been a more unfortunate  contretemps , and there is no telling how
disastrous the effect might have been, had not her courage and
coolness, not to say her orthodoxy, been equal to the occasion. She gave
her cousin a look which was still more terrible than Miss Bury's, and
then she took affairs into her own hands.
c7:p49.summary: The narrator emphasizes that a damaging social disaster has occurred, but Lucilla's courage, coolness, and orthodoxy allow her to take control and repair the situation.
c7:p49.best_quote: There could not have been a more unfortunate contretemps, and there is no telling how disastrous the effect might have been, had not her courage and coolness, not to say her orthodoxy, been equal to the occasion.

c8:p27.text:
She dreamed that she stood at the altar by the side
of the member for Carlingford, and that Mr Bury, with inflexible
cruelty, insisted upon marrying her to Tom Marjoribanks instead; and
then the scene changed, and instead of receiving the salutations of Mr
Cavendish as M.P. for the borough, it was the amusing man, in the
character of the defeated candidate, who grinned and nodded at her, and
said from the hustings that he would never forget the luncheon that had
been his first introduction to Carlingford.
c8:p27.summary: Lucilla dreams of being forced to marry Tom instead of securing Mr Cavendish as M.P., and of public mockery about the luncheon incident.

c10:p74.text:
But this
evening there could be no mistake about it. The words were arrested on
the very lips of the talkers; Mrs Woodburn paused in the midst of doing
Lucilla, and, as we have before said, Mr Cavendish broke a flirtation
clean off at its most interesting moment.
c10:p74.summary: The duet shocks the assembly into complete silence: conversations freeze, Mrs Woodburn ceases her mimicry, Cavendish abandons his flirtation—an unmissable moment.
c10:p74.best_quote: The words were arrested on the very lips of the talkers; Mrs Woodburn paused in the midst of doing Lucilla, and, as we have before said, Mr Cavendish broke a flirtation clean off at its most interesting moment.

c11:p11.text:
"It was a great deal more than pleasant," said Mr Cavendish; "and as for
your conception of social politics, it is masterly," the future M.P.
added, in a tone which struck Lucilla as very significant; not that she
cared particularly about Mr Cavendish's meaning, but still, when a young
man who intends to go into Parliament congratulates a young lady upon
her statesmanlike views, and her conception of politics, it must be
confessed that it looks a little particular; and then, if that was what
he meant, it was no doubt Lucilla's duty to make up her mind.
c11:p11.summary: Mr Cavendish congratulates Lucilla on her statesmanlike views with a tone that suggests romantic interest, prompting Lucilla to recognize this may require her decision.
c11:p11.best_quote: your conception of social politics, it is masterly

c4:p42.text:
"I am afraid I have taken your seat, papa,"
said Miss Marjoribanks, with ingenuous sweetness. "But then I should
have had to move the urn, and all the things, and I thought you would
not mind." The Doctor said nothing but "Humph!" and even that in an
undertone; but he became aware all the same that he had abdicated,
without knowing it, and that the reins of state had been smilingly
withdrawn from his unconscious hands.
c4:p42.summary: Lucilla apologizes sweetly, claiming she simply wanted to spare him the trouble of moving the urn; the Doctor utters only "Humph!" but understands he has surrendered power.
c4:p42.best_quote: he became aware all the same that he had abdicated, without knowing it, and that the reins of state had been smilingly withdrawn from his unconscious hands

c23:p20.text:
With every step
that she took, Miss Marjoribanks became more and more herself. As we
have already said, it was a grand and inspiring sight; but then, to be
sure, as in the former case, her affections, fortunately, were not
engaged. She was not in love with the Archdeacon, any more than she had
been in love with Mr Cavendish;—though it is true, love is not
everything.
c23:p20.summary: The narrator clarifies that Lucilla's distress stems not from lost love but from bruised pride and wounded ambition.
c23:p20.best_quote: She was not in love with the Archdeacon, any more than she had been in love with Mr Cavendish;—though it is true, love is not everything.

c27:p65.text:
We mention this fact rather as a contribution to the
history of those phenomena of the human mind, which have as yet escaped
the metaphysician, than as an actual circumstance in the life of Miss
Marjoribanks. She was a woman of genius, and he only a very simple,
unlucky fellow; and yet a sensation of comfort came to Lucilla's heart
when she said "Poor Tom!"
c27:p65.summary: The narrator remarks that this psychological phenomenon—genius finding comfort in simple faith—is remarkable and deserves attention.
c27:p65.best_quote: She was a woman of genius, and he only a very simple, unlucky fellow; and yet a sensation of comfort came to Lucilla's heart when she said 'Poor Tom!'

c50:p49.text:
Fate and honest love had been waiting all the time till their
moment came; and now it was not even necessary to say anything about it. The fact was so clear that it did not require stating. It was to be Tom
after all.
c50:p49.summary: Fate and honest love have prevailed; Lucilla and Tom's outcome is now clear without need for further statement.
c50:p49.best_quote: It was to be Tom after all.

c50:p48.text:
It was to be Tom after all—after all the
archdeacons, doctors, generals, members of Parliament—after the ten
years and more in which she had not gone off—after the poor old
Doctor's grudge against the nephew whom he did not wish to inherit his
wealth, and Aunt Jemima's quiet wiles, and attempt to disappoint her
boy.
c50:p48.summary: The narrator catalogues the many suitors and obstacles Tom has overcome to finally win Lucilla.
c50:p48.best_quote: after all the archdeacons, doctors, generals, members of Parliament—after the ten years and more in which she had not gone off
